travel.meta.title: Annaya Online Tour: Walk Saint Charbel's Monastery
travel.meta.description: A guided online walk through Annaya in five stops: the monastery, the pilgrim church, the courtyard, the tomb, and the hermitage, with real photographs.
travel.header.harissa: Our Lady of Lebanon at Harissa
travel.hero.answer1: This is a guided walk through Annaya, the Lebanese mountain monastery where Saint Charbel lived and is buried. Scroll through five stops: the monastery, the church, the courtyard, the tomb, and the hermitage. Each has a real photograph and a short story of why it matters.
travel.hero.trailLink2: the full story of his life
travel.images.alt1: The church and monastery of Saint Maron at Annaya on a terraced mountainside in winter, with a bell tower and a red-tiled roof
travel.stop1.heading: The Monastery on the Mountain
travel.stop1.text1: Begin on the hillside. Annaya belongs to the Jbeil district, roughly 52 km north of Beirut. The monastery rests on a wooded slope near 1,200 m, and on a clear day the sea shows far below the terraces.
travel.stop1.why1: Charbel spent most of his grown life on this hill, and every stop that follows is a short walk from where you are standing.
travel.images.alt2: Night view from above of the Annaya church with its lit cross and the monastery buildings among the pines and village lights
travel.stop2.heading: The Church Built for the Pilgrims
travel.stop2.text1: Once Charbel was beatified in 1965, visitors came in far greater numbers than the old buildings could take. The Lebanese Maronite Order answered with a new, larger church, consecrated in 1974. The tomb itself lies in the vaulted Tomb Church nearby - stop 4 on this walk.
travel.stop2.why1: Its size tells you how many people still make the climb, especially on the 22nd of the month and at the July feast.
travel.images.alt3: The stone monastery courtyard at Annaya at night, with arched windows and a round stone fountain
travel.stop3.heading: The Courtyard
travel.stop3.text1: Every pilgrim passes through this courtyard on the way in. The walls are bare stone, the windows are arched, and a fountain murmurs in the middle. Nobody pays to enter, and nobody is asked what they believe.
travel.stop3.why1: People arrive talking and leave quiet. The place works on you before you have decided to pray.
travel.images.alt4: Arched tomb chamber at Annaya with a candle-lit icon of Saint Charbel above the reliquary
travel.stop4.heading: The Tomb
travel.stop4.text1: Here is what the climb is for. A line forms, and the people in it pray while they wait. Many hold a folded note with a name on it. When your turn comes there is nothing to perform: you kneel, you touch the stone if you wish, and you stay as long as you need.
travel.stop4.why1: For most visitors, this is the whole reason for the journey. More on
travel.images.alt5: View toward the coast and the sea from the hermitage area of Annaya, over a stone terrace and flat roof
travel.stop5.heading: The Hermitage of Saints Peter and Paul
travel.stop5.text1: A path leads up from the monastery to the hermitage of Saints Peter and Paul. This photograph, taken from the hermitage area and published on the monastery's own hermitage page, looks out over a terrace toward the sea. Charbel moved up here in 1875. He remained for twenty-three years, until he died on Christmas Eve 1898.
travel.stop5.why1: The tomb is where people go to ask him for help. The hermitage is where he did his own praying, alone. More on
